scenes.heading: Volume of prisms and cylinders
scenes.say: How much water fits in a tank, or how much juice is in a can? One simple idea finds the volume of every prism and cylinder. Let’s see how.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A loaf of identical bread slices
scenes.breaks: Real slices have gaps and crusts; maths slices are infinitely thin and fit perfectly.
scenes.say: Think of a loaf where every slice is exactly the same shape. The volume is the area of one slice times how long the loaf is. A prism or a cylinder works the same way: the same cross-section repeated all along.

scenes.heading: Same slice all the way along
scenes.say: Here is a prism. First the solid, then its end face, labelled A. That same shape runs all the way along. So the volume is A times the length.

scenes.heading: Cylinder volume
scenes.say: A cylinder has a circle for its cross-section, so its volume is pi r squared times h. If you are given the diameter, halve it first.

scenes.heading: Tank in litres
scenes.question: A cylindrical tank has diameter 2 m and height 1.5 m. How many litres does it hold?
scenes.say: Diameter two metres, so the radius is one. Pi times one squared times one point five is about four point seven one two cubic metres. Each cubic metre holds a thousand litres, so the tank holds about four thousand seven hundred and twelve litres.
scenes.caption: r = 1 m. V = π × 1² × 1.5 ≈ 4.7124 m³. 1 m³ = 1000 L, so about 4712 L.

scenes.heading: Capacity units
scenes.say: One cubic centimetre holds one millilitre. A thousand cubic centimetres is one litre. And one cubic metre holds a thousand litres.

scenes.heading: Hollow pipe: ring × length
scenes.say: Here is the end of a pipe. First the outer circle, radius five, then the hole, radius four. The ring is twenty-five pi minus sixteen pi, which is nine pi. Multiply by the length, one hundred centimetres, to get about two thousand eight hundred and twenty-seven point four cubic centimetres.
scenes.caption: Outer radius 5 cm, hole radius 4 cm. Ring = 25π − 16π = 9π cm². × 100 cm ≈ 2827.4 cm³.

scenes.say: Quick recap. For a prism, volume is the area of the end times the length. For a cylinder, pi r squared h. One litre is a thousand cubic centimetres and one cubic metre is a thousand litres. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: Prism: V = A × length. Cylinder: V = πr²h. 1 L = 1000 cm³; 1 m³ = 1000 L. Now try the practice questions!
